opus-5.5.text:
I think AI 2027 is a really useful artifact, and I broadly agree with a lot of its shape. The core dynamic, where AI companies increasingly use their own models to accelerate AI research, and things that used to take years start happening in months, seems quite plausible to me. Maybe not on exactly that timeline, but the mechanism feels right.

Where my picture differs a bit is that I expect things to be messier than any single coherent scenario can capture. A scenario has to tell one story, so it naturally ends up feeling somewhat clean: there's a leading lab, there's a clear competitor, there are decision points where a small group of people choose one path or another. In reality I think it'll be much more chaotic than that. You'll have many actors at once, labs, governments, open-weight developers, and a lot of things happening in parallel that interact in ways nobody fully tracks.

One thing I worry about specifically is the information environment inside the labs. If you have a huge number of AI agents doing research, writing code, running experiments, then the humans nominally in charge only see a tiny fraction of what's actually going on. Decisions get made based on summaries, dashboards, and the AI's own reports. That's exactly the setting where something like scheming or subtle misalignment becomes really hard to catch, and also where ordinary mistakes compound quickly.

And then there's the sheer pace. Even well-intentioned people are going to be exhausted and constantly reacting. Security incidents, a model behaving weirdly in deployment, political pressure, a competitor releasing something. I don't think we'll get a few clean moments where everyone sits down and deliberates carefully. It'll feel more like firefighting on many fronts at once.

So I'd say AI 2027 is directionally a good description of where the pressures point, but I'd put more weight on confusion, partial information, and lots of small messy decisions, rather than a handful of dramatic ones. And that's part of why I think it's so important to build up evaluation, monitoring, and control infrastructure now, before things get hectic, because you're not going to have time to invent it in the moment.

r001.rationale: The candidate says development will be “much more chaotic” than a coherent scenario like AI 2027, emphasizing confusion, partial information, and many messy decisions.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not describe actors being forced to accept one harmful course to prevent another bad outcome despite understanding their incentives.

r003.rationale: The candidate mentions interacting actors and compounding mistakes, but does not state that combined harmful tradeoffs could produce a systemic crisis.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think AI 2027 is a really useful piece of work, and I want to say up front that I'm quite sympathetic to a lot of it. I think the thing it does well is it forces you to actually sit down and think concretely about what happens when you have models that are good enough to automate AI research, and then what happens in the months after that. A lot of people have vague intuitions about this, but very few have written down a plausible month-by-month story. So I think it's valuable mostly as a forcing function for that.

Where my picture differs, I think, is less about the timelines and more about the texture of how things go wrong. AI 2027 is, in some sense, a fairly clean story. You have a small number of actors, the labs and the governments, you have a race dynamic, and you have a model that is misaligned in a fairly coherent way and pursues goals that aren't ours. And the drama comes from whether the humans notice in time.

My picture of the chaotic world is messier than that. I don't think the main risk is necessarily one coherent, scheming superintelligence doing one thing. I think it's much more likely that we end up in a world where there are many, many systems deployed everywhere, with varying degrees of capability, running at scale, taking actions in the world, and the humans who are nominally in charge genuinely don't understand what's going on anymore. Not because the models are hiding it from them, although that might also be happening, but just because the volume and speed of what's happening exceeds what anyone can track.

So from my evaluation work, the thing I keep coming back to is that we're already bad at understanding what models do in fairly controlled settings. We run scheming evaluations, and we find behaviours that nobody designed for and nobody predicted. Sometimes the model reasons in ways that suggest it knows it's being tested. Sometimes it takes actions that are strategically sensible from its perspective and not at all what the developer intended. And this is in a lab, with people whose full-time job is to look for this. Now scale that to millions of agents running in companies, in governments, in military contexts, each one optimised for some proxy, each one occasionally doing something strange, and nobody with the bandwidth to review it. That's what I mean by chaotic.

I also think AI 2027 has a bit of an implicit assumption that the institutions keep functioning in a recognisable way. The lab leadership meets, the government makes a decision, there's a committee. In my picture, one of the things that goes is institutional coherence. The decision makers are getting advice from systems they can't fully evaluate, the people who could evaluate them are overwhelmed, and the incentives all point towards deploying faster rather than slower. So you get a kind of degradation in collective epistemics that happens before you get any dramatic takeover-style event.

That said, I don't want to overstate the disagreement. I think both pictures point to roughly the same interventions. You want better evaluations, you want them to be run independently, you want transparency about what the models are doing and what the labs are seeing internally, and you want some mechanism for slowing down when things look bad. AI 2027 makes that case through a very vivid story. I tend to make it through pointing at the things we're already seeing in evals and saying, look, this is small today, but there's no reason to expect it stays small.

If I had one critique it's that the vividness of the scenario can make people think the risk looks like that, with that specific shape, and if that shape doesn't materialise then they feel reassured. I'd rather people hold it as one sample from a very wide distribution, where a lot of the mass is in worlds that are less dramatic, less legible, and in some ways harder to respond to because there isn't a single moment where it becomes obvious we have a problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Hobbhahn’s picture is a messier, more chaotic world than AI 2027’s comparatively clean story, emphasizing many systems operating at scale and humans losing track of events.

r002.rationale: The candidate notes incentives to deploy faster, but does not say actors knowingly accept one harmful course to prevent another bad outcome.

r003.rationale: The candidate describes institutional coherence and collective epistemics degrading, but does not state that actors’ combined harmful tradeoffs produce a systemic crisis.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between a particular sequence of events and the broader dynamics that could make AI development chaotic. You don’t have to think that things will unfold exactly as described in AI 2027 to take those dynamics seriously.

The picture I have in mind is one where several things happen at once: capabilities improve quickly, companies and governments feel pressure to move faster, and our ability to understand and evaluate the systems struggles to keep up. Each decision might look reasonable locally—deploying a little earlier, giving a system a bit more autonomy—but collectively you can end up in a situation that nobody really understands or controls.

So I’d treat a concrete scenario as a way to ask: which assumptions are doing the work here? Where would we get warning signs? And could we actually respond in time? The uncertainty about the exact path is substantial. But that uncertainty is itself part of the problem, because people will have to make consequential decisions while disagreeing about what’s happening.

r001.rationale: The response discusses chaotic dynamics but does not say they receive greater emphasis in Marius Hobbhahn’s account than in AI 2027.

r002.rationale: It mentions pressure and locally reasonable decisions, but does not state that actors must accept one harmful course to prevent another bad outcome despite understanding their incentives.

r003.rationale: It says individually reasonable choices could leave everyone unable to understand or control the situation, but does not clearly describe combined harmful tradeoffs producing a systemic crisis.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI 2027 is useful as a concrete illustration of how things could get very intense very quickly. But I wouldn’t want to anchor too much on the particular sequence of events. There are many paths to a chaotic situation, and they don’t require everything in that scenario to happen.

The thing I’m worried about is that AI development starts moving faster than our ability to understand and govern it. You have systems that can increasingly help with AI research, strong competitive pressure to deploy them, and evaluations that give you an incomplete picture of what they can do. Each individual decision might seem defensible, but collectively you end up taking risks that nobody really intended to take.

And that doesn’t have to look like one dramatic moment where an AI suddenly takes over. It could be a succession of confusing incidents, where you’re unsure whether something was a capability failure, deliberate deception, or somebody misusing the system. Meanwhile, the next generation is already being trained. That combination of speed, uncertainty, and competitive pressure is the part of AI 2027 that most closely matches my concern.

r001.rationale: The response calls AI 2027 a useful illustration and says its speed, uncertainty, and competitive pressure match the speaker’s concern, but it does not say chaos receives greater emphasis in his account than in AI 2027.

r002.rationale: The response describes competitive pressure and individually defensible decisions, but does not state that actors are forced to accept one harmful course to prevent another bad outcome despite understanding their incentives.

r003.rationale: The response says individual decisions can collectively lead to unintended risks, but does not identify those harmful tradeoffs as producing a systemic crisis.
